In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of HPV vaccines.
understanding HPV immunobiology and the immune response to HPV infection, in particular the cellular immune response.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the two commercial HPV VLP vaccines are highly effective in preventing cervical pre-cancer, and therefore, presumably, cervical cancer, in women who have not been previously exposed to the HPV types in the vaccine.

vaccination with HPV VLP vaccines has been demonstrated effective in the prevention of cervical precancer associated with the HPV types in the vaccine, and in preventing infection with the same types, over a period of 3 to 4 years in young women.
HPV vaccines are effective at preventing HPV infections with the HPV types included in the vaccine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the development of the HPV vaccines, from the initial proposal that the virus could be the cause of cervical cancer, to the first licensure of an effective vaccine in the developed world, took 25 years.

the HPV vaccines are effective, and safe, at preventing infection with vaccine targeted HPV types, but that the efficacy at preventing progression of infection to cervical pre-cancer has been less well established.

the natural history of HR HPV infections is much more dynamic than was appreciated prior to the development of the HPV VLP vaccines, and that the vaccines have allowed us to better understand the dynamics of the natural history.
